prompt: Which workload does storing by column suit?
hint: A few columns of every row.

choices.text: The report's
choices.why: Right. The columns it uses are each one stretch of disk.

choices.text: The till's, which writes and reads whole rows by key
choices.why: A whole row is in eleven places in a column store.

choices.text: Both equally, since the data is the same
choices.why: The layout favours one or the other.

choices.text: Neither; it is about saving disk only
choices.why: Space is a consequence; reading less is the point.

prompt: The fact table took 79 MB in PostgreSQL and 9,449,472 bytes in DuckDB. Roughly how many times smaller is the DuckDB file? Give a whole number.
Why is PostgreSQL's table larger even than the CSV text of the same rows?
hint: What does each row carry for the till?

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps two copies of every table, one for reading and one for writing
choices.why: It keeps one; the size is per row.

choices.text: The CSV file was compressed
choices.why: It was plain text.

choices.text: Row headers, full-width numbers and free space
choices.why: Right. The costs of a store built for transactions.

choices.text: PostgreSQL stores numbers as text
choices.why: It stores them as binary integers.

prompt: To sum `net_cents`, how much of the PostgreSQL table did it read?

choices.text: One eleventh, one column of eleven
choices.why: That is what a column store would read.

choices.text: All of it
choices.why: Right. 10,144 of 10,144 pages: the column is spread through every row.

choices.text: Only the pages that were not in memory
choices.why: It read those and the ones in memory: 8,064 plus 2,080.

choices.text: Only the index on `net_cents`
choices.why: There is no index on that column.

prompt: `net_cents` takes 1,119,464 of the Parquet file's 9,492,481 bytes. What percentage of the file does summing it read? Give a whole number.
How does dictionary encoding store a column of shop keys?

choices.text: The value and how many times it repeats in a row
choices.why: That is run-length encoding.

choices.text: Each value as its distance from the minimum
choices.why: That is frame of reference.

choices.text: As text, alphabetically
choices.why: Order and type are not the trick.

choices.text: Each value once, plus a small code per row
choices.why: Right. Seven shops need three bits per row.

prompt: Why did DuckDB choose RLE for every segment of `date_key`?

choices.text: Dates are always stored that way
choices.why: In the shuffled file the same column was a megabyte.

choices.text: The column was declared with RLE
choices.why: Nobody declared an encoding; DuckDB tried them.

choices.text: Each day's sales sit together, in long runs
choices.why: Right. Loaded by order number, which rises with time.

choices.text: `date_key` has the most distinct values
choices.why: It has 731, far fewer than order_id.

prompt: Match each encoding to what it exploits.
hint: Few values, runs, or a narrow range.

pairs.right: Equal values next to each other
Values that fit in few bits

prompt: `quantity` is always 1, 2 or 3. How many bits does each value need?
A column is declared `BIGINT` but holds only small numbers. What does that cost in a column store?

choices.text: Almost nothing extra
choices.why: Right. Bit-packing looks at the values, not the declared type.

choices.text: Eight bytes per row, as declared
choices.why: That is the row store's cost.

choices.text: Twice as much as a 32-bit integer, always
choices.why: The encoding ignores the declared width.

choices.text: It is refused by the engine
choices.why: Every engine accepts it.

prompt: Storing a block's minimum once and each value as its distance from it is called frame of ___.
Why did `title` get FSST and not a dictionary?

choices.text: Titles are too long for any dictionary
choices.why: Length is not the problem; uniqueness is.

choices.text: FSST is used for every text column
choices.why: `department` and `format` got a dictionary.

choices.text: Titles are in English
choices.why: The language does not matter to the encoding.

choices.text: Titles are almost all different, but share fragments
choices.why: Right. A dictionary of whole titles would be as large as the column.

prompt: Sorted by shop and date, `shop_key` took 524 bytes. Why so little?

choices.text: Shop keys were dropped from the sorted file
choices.why: All 887,477 values are there.

choices.text: Seven runs, one per shop
choices.why: Right. Run-length encoding at its best.

choices.text: Sorting converts integers to text
choices.why: Types do not change.

choices.text: Parquet compresses small integers to zero bytes when they are sorted
choices.why: Not zero: 524 bytes, the cost of seven runs and their counts.

prompt: Shuffled, the file took 13,403,406 bytes; in order of order number, 9,331,332. By what percentage did the order shrink it? Give a whole number.
hint: The saving over the shuffled size.

prompt: Order the three files by their total size, largest first.
trap: The two sorted files are close; the shuffled one is about 40% larger than either.

prompt: What is a zone map?

choices.text: Each block's minimum and maximum
choices.why: Right. A reader discards blocks whose range misses the filter.

choices.text: An index on every value of a column, kept in a separate B-tree
choices.why: That is a conventional index, which a zone map is not.

choices.text: A map of which node holds which rows
choices.why: That is distribution, lesson 7.

choices.text: A list of the folders a table is split into
choices.why: That is partitioning.

prompt: In the file ordered by order number, how many of the 8 row groups could hold a sale from March 2025?
The shuffled file has the same data, yet every row group must be read for March. Why?

choices.text: Shuffled files have no statistics
choices.why: They have them; the statistics are just useless.

choices.text: DuckDB ignores zone maps on Parquet
choices.why: It used them on the ordered file.

choices.text: Every group spans both years, so none is ruled out
choices.why: Right. Zone maps need the rows a query wants to sit together.

choices.text: March has no sales in that file
choices.why: It has the same sales.

prompt: Match each part of a Parquet file to what it is.

pairs.right: Schema and per-block metadata, read first
One column's values inside a row group

prompt: Why does a Parquet reader read the footer first?
hint: What does it need before reading data?

choices.text: The footer holds the first rows
choices.why: It holds metadata, not rows.

choices.text: To know where everything is, and what to skip
choices.why: Right. Positions, sizes, encodings and min/max per block.

choices.text: To check a password
choices.why: Parquet has no password in the footer.

choices.text: Because files are written backwards
choices.why: Data comes first; the metadata is written at the end.

prompt: A table in Parquet must have 5,000 rows corrected. What does that involve?
hint: Parquet has no notion of change.

choices.text: An UPDATE on the file, in place
choices.why: Files are written once, whole, and never edited.

choices.text: Changing the footer's statistics
choices.why: The statistics describe data that would still be wrong.

choices.text: Nothing; Parquet corrects itself
choices.why: Nothing corrects data by itself.

choices.text: Rewriting the files that hold them
choices.why: Right. A changing table is many files and a record of which are current: lesson 10.

prompt: Which of these make vectorised execution fast? Choose all that apply.
hint: A batch of one column at a time.

choices.text: Overhead paid once per vector, not per row
choices.why: Yes. 2,048 values per call in DuckDB.

choices.text: Contiguous values that fill the cache with useful data
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Instructions that work on several values at once
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: An index on every column
choices.why: Vectorised scans need no index.

prompt: What is late materialisation?

choices.text: Loading the warehouse at night
choices.why: That is a schedule.

choices.text: Refreshing a materialised view late
choices.why: Different word, different idea.

choices.text: Fetching other columns only for rows that survive the filter
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Decompressing everything before filtering
choices.why: The opposite: work on compressed data where possible.

prompt: Two thousand single-row inserts took 0.956 s in PostgreSQL and 1.981 s in DuckDB. Why is the column store slower here?

choices.text: Each row is split across every column's block
choices.why: Right. Two thousand times, each durably.

choices.text: DuckDB checks every row against every other
choices.why: There is no such check on a table without constraints.

choices.text: DuckDB inserts are always slow, whatever their size
choices.why: Batch loads are its strength; single rows are the problem.

choices.text: PostgreSQL skips writing to disk
choices.why: It writes; a row append is simply cheaper.

prompt: DuckDB found order 112406 in 0.002 s with no index. Why would a lookup by `customer_key` be a different story?

choices.text: Customer keys are encrypted
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted here.

choices.text: There are fewer customers than orders
choices.why: The count is not what matters; the order is.

choices.text: Customer keys are not integers
choices.why: They are integers.

choices.text: The table is sorted by order, not by customer
choices.why: Right. Every block would contain customers of every range, so none could be skipped.

prompt: A table has 50 columns and a report reads 3 of them over every row. Which store reads less, and roughly how much less?
hint: Bytes of the columns used, against bytes of whole rows.

choices.text: The row store, because it reads each row once from start to finish
choices.why: Reading each row once means reading all 50 columns.

choices.text: The column store, by an order of magnitude or more
choices.why: Right. Three columns of fifty, before compression even starts.

choices.text: Both read the same, since every row is needed
choices.why: Every row, but not every column.

choices.text: The row store, if it has an index on the three
choices.why: An index helps find rows, not read every row's columns.

prompt: Most queries on a fact table filter by month and then by shop. Which order should its rows be written in?
hint: Rows a query wants should sit together.

choices.text: By date, then shop
choices.why: Right. Zone maps skip most months, and shops cluster inside each.

choices.text: Shuffled, so that every node and block gets an even mix of the data
choices.why: Even mixing is what makes zone maps useless.

choices.text: By customer, which has the most distinct values of any key
choices.why: Many values suit a distribution key; sort by what queries filter on.

choices.text: By net amount, largest first
choices.why: Nobody filters by it; it would scatter dates across every block.
